ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) -- Eight cadets and staff members were killed in Pakistan during an an eight-hour standoff Monday with gunmen who stormed a police training center in Lahore, said Gen. Athar Abbas, a military spokesman. Police fire into the air after retaking the police training center in Lahore attacked by militants. The militants had been holed up on the top floor of a three-story building, said Rehman Malik, the head of the country's Interior Ministry. Security forces gained control of the first two floors and eventually made their way to the top, finally taking control of it and arresting the gunmen Monday afternoon. Television pictures showed security forces firing into the air from the roof of the building after the firefight. "The operation is over. Four terrorists were killed and three arrested," Interior Ministry Secretary Kamal Shah told Reuters. Malik and Abbas confirmed the figures. Abbas added some of the dead militants blew themselves up. The gang of seven gunmen stormed the academy in the Manawan area of the eastern Pakistani city, said Malik. Abbas had previously said 30 people were killed. He cited the error on wrong information by his sources at the scene.  Watch more about the attack » . At a news conference Monday night, Malik named the leader of the Pakistani Taliban, Baitullah Mehsud, and his followers as the prime suspect in organizing the attack. Mehsud is also accused of plotting the assassination of former PM Benazir Bhutto. At least 78 people were wounded in the attack, authorities said. Lahore is the same city where gunmen opened fire March 10 on a bus carrying members of the Sri Lankan national cricket team on their way to a stadium for a match. The well-coordinated attack wounded at least eight members of the team and killed a driver and six Pakistani police officers. In Monday's incident, the attackers hurled grenades, then stormed the compound and opened fire while officers were taking part in their morning drill. About 800 officers train at the facility, but authorities could not say exactly how many were inside at the time. The attackers, some in police uniforms, took dozens of officers hostage, said Asim Rizwan, spokesman for governor of Punjab -- the province where Lahore is located. Paramilitary forces and the army descended on the scene. Every few minutes, the gunmen detonated explosives or fired on reporters and police personnel outside, sending them scurrying for cover. Angry onlookers pumped their fists in the air and cheered as police led away a suspect they had captured. He had on him a grenade and a knife, officials told CNN. CNN's Reza Sayah contributed to this report.

# Eight Killed in Standoff at Pakistani Police Academy

ISLAMABAD, Pakistan (CNN) -- Eight cadets and staff members were killed during an eight-hour standoff in Lahore, Pakistan, on Monday, when gunmen stormed a police training center, according to Gen. Athar Abbas, a military spokesman.

The militants had taken refuge on the top floor of a three-story building, said Rehman Malik, head of the country's Interior Ministry. Security forces first secured the lower two floors before advancing to the top level, ultimately regaining full control of the facility and apprehending the assailants Monday afternoon. Television footage showed security personnel firing celebratory shots into the air from the rooftop following the confrontation.

"The operation is over. Four terrorists were killed and three arrested," Interior Ministry Secretary Kamal Shah told Reuters. Both Malik and Abbas corroborated these figures, with Abbas noting that some of the slain militants had detonated explosives on themselves.

According to Malik, a group of seven gunmen launched the assault on the academy located in the Manawan area of eastern Lahore. Abbas had earlier reported a death toll of 30, an error he attributed to inaccurate information relayed by sources at the scene.

At a Monday evening press conference, Malik identified Baitullah Mehsud, leader of the Pakistani Taliban, along with his followers, as the principal suspects behind the attack's planning. Mehsud has also been implicated in the assassination plot against former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto.

Authorities reported that at least 78 people were injured in the assault.

This marks the second high-profile attack in Lahore in recent months. On March 10, gunmen opened fire on a bus transporting members of the Sri Lankan national cricket team as it traveled to a stadium for a match. That coordinated assault left at least eight team members wounded and claimed the lives of a driver and six Pakistani police officers.

In Monday's attack, assailants first hurled grenades before storming the compound and opening fire as officers were engaged in morning drills. Approximately 800 officers train at the facility, though authorities could not confirm the exact number present during the assault.

Some attackers, disguised in police uniforms, took dozens of officers hostage, according to Asim Rizwan, spokesman for the governor of Punjab province, where Lahore is situated. Paramilitary units and army forces swiftly converged on the scene. Throughout the standoff, the gunmen periodically detonated explosives or fired upon reporters and police personnel stationed outside, forcing them to repeatedly seek cover.

As police escorted away a captured suspect—found carrying a grenade and a knife, officials told CNN—angry onlookers raised their fists and cheered in a display of defiance.

*CNN's Reza Sayah contributed to this report.*

**LAHORE, Pakistan** — Militants armed with automatic weapons and explosives stormed a police training academy on the outskirts of Lahore early Monday, triggering a gun battle that lasted for hours before security forces regained control of the compound, officials said.

At least 29 people were killed and more than 130 others wounded in the assault, according to Punjab provincial health officials, though authorities cautioned that the toll could rise as search teams continued clearing the sprawling academy grounds.

## Attack Unfolds at Dawn

Witnesses said the attackers — believed to number between four and six — breached the perimeter of the facility around 5:30 a.m. local time, just as hundreds of police recruits were gathering for morning drills. Officials said the gunmen opened fire indiscriminately before taking dozens of cadets hostage inside two dormitory buildings.

"We heard explosions first, then heavy gunfire," said one recruit who escaped over a rear wall during the initial chaos. "There was no time to think. Everyone was just running."

Pakistani security forces, including army commandos and elite police units, surrounded the compound within the hour and began an operation to clear the buildings room by room. The standoff stretched for nearly eight hours, punctuated by intermittent gunfire and at least two suicide blasts believed to have been detonated by the attackers as forces closed in.

## Officials Confirm End of Siege

By mid-afternoon, Punjab's police chief announced that all attackers had been "neutralized" and the facility was fully secured. Three militants were reportedly killed by security forces, while at least one detonated an explosive vest.

"This was a cowardly attack on those who dedicate their lives to protecting our citizens," a senior Interior Ministry official said at a press briefing. "We will not be intimidated."

## Claims of Responsibility

A faction linked to Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) claimed responsibility for the attack in a statement issued to media outlets, though Pakistani officials said they were still working to verify the claim and investigate possible links to other militant networks operating in the region.

This is not the first time security installations in Punjab province have been targeted. Analysts note that police and paramilitary training centers have increasingly become targets for militant groups seeking to undermine public confidence in Pakistan's security apparatus.

## Aftermath and Response

Hospitals across Lahore were placed on emergency alert as ambulances ferried the wounded throughout the morning. Local blood banks issued urgent appeals as supplies ran low.

Pakistani Prime Minister's office condemned the attack in a statement, calling it "an attack on the state itself," and pledged that those responsible — including any who provided logistical support — would be brought to justice.

International reaction was swift, with the United States, United Kingdom, and United Nations issuing statements condemning the violence and offering condolences to the victims' families.

Authorities have not released the names of those killed pending notification of relatives. An investigation into how the attackers breached a facility with reportedly tight security remains ongoing.

---
*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

**LAHORE, Pakistan** — Heavily armed militants stormed a police training facility in an assault that plunged the compound into chaos for nearly eight hours before security forces regained control, according to officials who described a coordinated and carefully planned operation.

## Timeline of the Attack

The assault began in the early morning hours, when gunmen — reportedly numbering between four and ten, according to varying official accounts — approached the training center from multiple directions. Witnesses described the attackers scaling walls and opening fire on cadets who were gathered for morning exercises, catching many recruits in the open and unprotected.

Within minutes, explosions echoed through the compound as militants tossed grenades into barracks and administrative buildings. Police and paramilitary forces scrambled to seal off the perimeter, but the attackers had already taken up defensive positions inside, using trainees as hostages and shields.

By mid-morning, army commandos and elite police units had surrounded the facility, exchanging sporadic gunfire with the militants holed up inside. The standoff stretched through the afternoon as security forces methodically cleared room by room, wary of explosives the attackers were believed to be carrying.

Smoke could be seen rising from the compound for hours as sporadic gunfire and explosions punctuated the siege. By the time the operation concluded roughly eight hours after it began, several militants had been killed, with reports indicating at least one may have detonated a suicide vest rather than be captured.

## Casualties and Aftermath

Officials confirmed a significant number of casualties among police recruits and trainers, with dozens more wounded. The exact toll remained fluid in the hours after the operation ended, as rescue workers continued pulling bodies and survivors from the wreckage.

## Official Response

**Rehman Malik**, then serving as Pakistan's Interior Minister, condemned the attack in a televised statement, calling it "an attempt to destabilize the internal security of the country" and vowing that "the terrorists will not succeed in their nefarious designs." Malik pledged a thorough investigation and suggested the attack bore the hallmarks of banned militant networks operating from Pakistan's tribal areas.

"This is a war imposed upon us," Malik said. "We will fight it and we will win it."

**Maj. Gen. Athar Abbas**, the military's chief spokesman, provided details on the operation's execution, praising the coordination between army commandos and police units. He emphasized that troops had exercised caution to minimize casualties among the trainee hostages, saying forces "moved deliberately to save as many lives as possible" rather than launching an immediate full-scale assault.

Abbas also addressed questions about the militants' origins and planning, stating that initial evidence suggested the attackers had studied the compound's layout in advance and may have had insider knowledge of the facility's security arrangements — a claim that raised uncomfortable questions about potential vulnerabilities within security ranks.

## Broader Implications

The attack added to a mounting series of assaults on security installations across Pakistan, underscoring the persistent threat faced by law enforcement and military personnel even within fortified compounds. Analysts noted the operation's complexity — the use of multiple attackers, hostage-taking, and apparent reconnaissance — pointed to a level of planning consistent with previous high-profile militant operations in the region.

Officials pledged reviews of security protocols at training installations nationwide, though skepticism lingered among residents and opposition figures about whether such promises would translate into meaningful reform.

---

**Gunmen Storm Pakistani Police Academy, Battle Security Forces in Hours-Long Siege**

LAHORE, Pakistan (AP) — Heavily armed militants stormed a police training academy on the outskirts of this eastern Pakistani city Monday, triggering a gun battle with security forces that stretched for more than eight hours before ending with the attackers dead or in custody.

Officials said between eight and 12 gunmen, some wearing suicide vests and police-style uniforms, scaled the walls of the Manawan Police Training School before dawn and opened fire on cadets gathered for morning parade drills. The attackers took control of parts of the sprawling compound, holding dozens of recruits hostage inside dormitory buildings as the siege unfolded.

"They came in through the back wall and started shooting immediately," said one police trainee who escaped over a perimeter fence, speaking on condition of anonymity. "There was no warning."

Police and paramilitary Rangers surrounded the facility within minutes and exchanged gunfire with the attackers throughout the morning. Explosions were heard periodically as the standoff continued, and thick smoke rose from at least one building believed to have been set ablaze during the fighting.

By early afternoon, officials said security forces had regained control of most of the compound, though sporadic gunfire continued from a rooftop position where two attackers had barricaded themselves with a small number of hostages.

**Casualties**

The Punjab provincial government said at least eight people were killed in the attack, including police cadets and instructors, with more than 95 others wounded, many of them cadets caught in the initial crossfire. Officials cautioned that the death toll could rise as forces cleared the remaining buildings.

Of the attackers, authorities said at least four were killed during the operation, three detonated explosive vests rather than surrender, and several others were captured alive. Interior Ministry officials said interrogations of the surviving attackers were underway to determine the group responsible.

**Resolution**

The siege ended shortly before 3 p.m. local time when commandos from the Elite Police Force breached the final holdout position, killing the remaining gunmen and freeing the last of the hostages unharmed. Officials said the rescued cadets were taken to nearby hospitals for treatment of minor injuries and shock.

Punjab Law Minister Rana Sanaullah told reporters at the scene that the operation had been "brought to a successful conclusion" but acknowledged security lapses had allowed the attackers to breach the academy's perimeter.

"This was a well-planned and coordinated assault," Sanaullah said. "We are looking into how such a large group of armed men was able to enter a police facility undetected."

No group immediately claimed responsibility, though officials said the attack bore similarities to previous assaults linked to militant networks operating in the country's northwest. Pakistani security forces have faced a rising number of attacks on law enforcement and military installations in recent years amid ongoing operations against militant strongholds near the Afghan border.

Prime Minister Yousuf Raza Gilani condemned the attack and ordered an investigation into the security breach, calling it "an attack not just on the police, but on the state itself."

The academy, located in the Manawan area on Lahore's outskirts, trains thousands of police recruits annually and has not previously been the target of a major militant assault.

___

This story will be updated as more information becomes available.
